new_statements.quote: With respect to stress, Vilera Díaz (1985) makes some preliminary observations, suggesting that, while stress placement on nouns is difficult to account for, stress on demonstratives is consistently placed on the final syllable [...] note that the nouns have different stress patterns – penult for examples (a–c) and (e) versus final stress for (f–h) – while the demonstratives always have the stress on the final syllable [p. 557] [...] Based on this contrast, she suggests that Jodï stress may be phonemic [...] Additional minimal pairs are, however, available. Quatra (2008a: 26) explains that stress is not represented in the writing system unless it is needed to disambiguate two words [p. 558]
new_statements.citation: Rosés Labrada, Jorge Emilio. 2023. Jodï. In Patience Epps & Lev Michael (eds.), Amazonian Languages: Language Isolates I: Aikanã to Kandozi-Shapra, 548-613. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton. DOI 10.1515/9783110419405-012 (author's deposit, published layout, University of Alberta ERA, DOI 10.7939/r3-pyxe-ty88).
new_statements.locator: Section 3 Phonology, pp. 557-558 (Tables 12.9 and 12.10 and surrounding text; footnote 11 on p. 558)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (68 pp., text layer, published De Gruyter layout, running head "12 Jodï", DOI 10.1515/9783110419405-012 printed on p. 547). Section 3 Phonology, printed pp. 557-558 = PDF pages 11-12. Every segment of the reader's quote is there verbatim: p. 557 "With respect to stress, Vilera Díaz (1985) makes some preliminary observations, suggesting that, while stress placement on nouns is difficult to account for, stress on demonstratives is consistently placed on the final syllable and proposing that it is also used to disambiguate cases where a noun has the same form as the demonstrative.... note that the nouns have different stress patterns – penult for examples (a–c) and (e) versus final stre…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is not predictable from the segmental form: disyllabic nouns and verbs show either penultimate (initial) or final stress, and Table 12.10 (from Quatra 2008a: 26) gives nine minimal pairs contrasting penultimate vs final stress (e.g. ˈbaba 'father' vs baˈba 'classifier for flat things'; ˈbude 'whistle' vs buˈde 'light a fire'; ˈnuwɛ̃ 'go back' vs nuˈwẽ 'house'), so stress is treated as (probably) phonemic. One morphological regularity: demonstratives always carry final stress, which can disambiguate a noun from a homophonous demonstrative (ˈmĩhi 'calabash' vs mĩˈhi demonstrative+classifier). Vilera Díaz's noun examples split between penult (buˈhʷãmbo, ˈnãla, ˈbʷɛlo, ˈmĩhi) and final (nõˈnõ, doˈdo, mõʰˈto). The author states that prosody 'require[s] further research'. Contrasting earlier view: Guarisma Pinto (1974: 49) preliminarily judged stress and vowel length non-contrastive (reported in Rosés Labrada 2019, supplemental appendix p. 8, file).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned. Table 12.9 (d) ˈmẽʰnãheʰˈta 'shoe' carries two stress marks (as transcribed from Vilera Díaz 1985) but the text does not comment on it.
new_statements.exceptions: Footnote 11 (p. 558): Quatra's orthography marks stress only in the first column of the minimal pairs; the author inferred final stress for the unmarked partners, which he notes is problematic for the trisyllabic ãmi-ˈhã 'coroba grub'. Guarisma Pinto (1974) instead claimed pre-aspiration occurs 'automatically in pre-stressed positions' and that stress is not contrastive.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms (isolated words from elicited wordlists/dictionary; no texts exist). The chapter is explicitly a philological sketch based on secondary data (Vilera Díaz 1985, Quatra 2008a/b, Guarisma Pinto 1974/1978) plus the author's listening to Mattei Müller's AILLA audio; the stress observations are taken from Vilera Díaz 1985: 38-39 and Quatra 2008a: 26.
new_statements.identity_note: Rosés Labrada 2023 covers Jodï as a whole (San José de Kayamá and Caño Iguana communities); no dialect split is described. Glottolog yuwa1244 = Hoti/Jodï; the on-disk directory hoti1237 is a different, unrelated language (name coincidence only).
